Democrats’ Private Suicide Watch

Kevin JacksonNovember 3, 2026
6 minutes read

Who Would You Rather Be on Election Day?

Democrats want another election about Trump’s personality. Voters have questions about missing money, unfinished promises, and the people demanding another term to explain why nothing is their fault.

Explore Politics

If I were a Democrat, I’d have a psychiatrist on speed dial today. And before lying down on the couch, I’d check underneath it. At this point, another scandal could roll out.

It’s midterm Election Day, and I have a question: Who would you rather be?

Before you answer, imagine you’re responsible for explaining the Democratic Party’s record to somebody who hasn’t been watching your preferred television network. Somebody who still believes a government program ought to produce the thing printed on the brochure.

You’re explaining California’s railroad. Minnesota’s missing money. Your position on immigration enforcement. And somewhere in this conversation, you’ve got to explain why the real threat to the country is Donald Trump’s temperament.

That is quite a presentation. Particularly when the audience has already paid to see that show.

For years, Democrats have approached elections with a familiar understanding: Find an issue that frightens people, put Trump’s face next to it, and wait for the ballots. Abortion. Democracy. Whatever emergency requires them to retain power until further notice.

But what happens when voters begin asking follow-up questions?

You say you’re protecting vulnerable people. Fine. Where did the money intended for vulnerable people go?

You say government needs more resources. All right. What happened to the resources we already provided?

You say Trump threatens institutions. Would these be the institutions whose failures we aren’t supposed to question because questioning them threatens institutions?

Track Exec Orders

My contention is that Democrats have accumulated obligations they can no longer refinance with another speech about Trump. Eventually, somebody wants to inspect the collateral.

That somebody is the voter.

Now, I’m not telling you every Republican is wonderful. I’ve met Republicans. Some of them can turn a winning argument into a subcommittee. Give them a smoking gun and they’ll spend six months negotiating the font on the subpoena.

I’m asking you to compare what the parties need voters to believe.

Republicans can point to failed oversight, wasted money, and government agencies that require more supervision than the people they regulate.

Democrats must explain why those failures justify keeping their party in charge.

Explore Politics

Which argument requires more imagination?

The Children Were Hungry. Apparently, So Were the Adults.

Consider Minnesota.

The state’s legislative auditor concluded that the Department of Education’s inadequate oversight of Feeding Our Future created opportunities for fraud. The findings included missed warning signs, inadequate investigations, and failures to follow through on serious concerns. That is an official assessment of government performance.

That should be  politically devastating in a country where people are expected to perform the jobs for which they are paid.

How much failure can occur under your supervision before supervision becomes an issue?

Imagine hiring somebody to watch your house. You come home and the television is gone, the furniture is gone, and he says, “The important thing is that I remain committed to home security.”

Then he asks for a raise because your house has become a challenging environment.

Democrats have become remarkably skilled at describing the importance of a mission after the money for accomplishing it disappears. They can deliver a moving speech about hungry children. Apparently, producing a reliable accounting is where the compassion gets complicated.

Explore Politics

Every tax dollar has an owner. Before government spent it, somebody earned it. When somebody steals it, there are at least two victims: the person who provided it and the person who was supposed to receive the help.

That’s why I reject the idea that questioning a program means opposing the people it serves.

If you care about hungry children, you should be furious when their food money disappears. Your curiosity shouldn’t depend on whether the investigation will produce an awkward campaign commercial.

There is also a distinction voters understand perfectly well: Criminal responsibility belongs to those who commit crimes.  Political responsibility includes the people entrusted with preventing them.

A governor doesn’t have to be carrying the stolen television to answer questions about who was watching the house.

California Has Successfully Transported the Deadline

Discover more

politics
Republican Party history

Then there’s California’s high-speed railroad.

The rail authority’s own 2026 business-plan materials anticipate passenger service between Merced and Bakersfield beginning in 2033.

California has built a remarkable transportation system for moving expectations into the future.

The deadline gets there ahead of everybody.

Supporters can explain construction phases, financing structures, environmental reviews, procurement, and all the other reasons taxpayers should remain patient. Some of those explanations may describe real obstacles. But describing an obstacle is not the same as overcoming one, especially when overcoming obstacles was supposedly included in the job.

Try this in your business.

Promise a customer a product. Collect money. Miss the delivery. Explain that delivery requires additional money. Then tell the customer that the continued existence of your project proves its success.

Eventually, your customer stops admiring your commitment.

Democrats enjoy treating California as the laboratory for enlightened government. Fair enough. Voters are entitled to examine what came out of the laboratory.

Explore Politics

At some point, the experiment has to do more than consume funding and issue progress reports.

About Those Institutions

Now consider the demand that Americans trust the judgment of the institutions that investigated Trump.

The Justice Department inspector general identified 17 significant inaccuracies and omissions across the Carter Page surveillance applications by the final renewal. His testimony described failures to meet basic accuracy obligations in an investigation of extraordinary sensitivity.

Those findings do not require embellishment. Seventeen significant inaccuracies and omissions are quite capable of embarrassing themselves.

Yet Democrats still act mystified when Americans want receipts before accepting another solemn assurance from an official standing behind a seal.

Explore Politics

Trust is earned through conduct. You cannot repeatedly ask people to ignore documented failures and then diagnose their skepticism as a character defect.

Discover more

If a bank repeatedly mishandled your account, you’d move your money. Washington’s preferred response is to investigate why you’ve become hostile to banking.

And somehow Trump’s tone remains the emergency.

Apparently, Americans can survive institutions getting consequential things wrong. What we may never recover from is somebody discussing it impolitely.

Compassion Needs a Receipt

Immigration presents a similar problem for Democrats.

Explore Politics

They want voters to see compassion. Voters are entitled to ask how that compassion operates: Who enters? Who stays? Who pays? What happens when somebody violates the law? What obligation does government owe the citizens already here?

Those are ordinary governing questions. They don’t become immoral because an activist dislikes the answers.

When Democrats oppose an enforcement action, they should explain the alternative clearly enough that a parent, a mayor, and a taxpayer can understand who becomes responsible for the consequences.

“Trump is cruel” doesn’t answer any of those questions.

Neither does accusing everybody who asks them of secretly hating immigrants. Americans have relatives, neighbors, employees, and friends who immigrated here. Many have watched those people spend years meeting requirements that politicians now discuss as though compliance were an unfortunate personality trait.

The issue is whether government can enforce a coherent policy and explain it honestly.

That should be a manageable assignment for people campaigning to run the government.

Renew the Contract?

I’m not predicting that every Democrat loses. I’m asking readers to recognize how much of the Democratic argument depends on changing the subject.

There are only so many times you can tell the customer the roof leak is less important than the plumber’s attitude.

There are only so many investigations, missed deadlines, vanished dollars, and institutional failures you can stack behind a podium before “But Trump” begins sounding like an admission that the rest of the speech is unavailable.

My expectation is that more voters are reaching that point.

They can dislike something Trump says and still prefer his approach. They can recognize Republican shortcomings and still decide Democrats have exhausted their excuses. They can care about vulnerable people enough to demand that money intended for those people actually reaches them.

None of that requires an ideological conversion. Sometimes it requires opening the bill.

So, who would you rather be today?

The party arguing that government needs accountability?

Or the party explaining why accountability must wait until after another election?

Democrats can discuss Trump’s temperament with their psychiatrists.

Voters have a contract to renew.
